reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: An acquired epileptic aphasia in which a previously normally developing child loses language, typically between three and eight years of age
The hallmark is acquired verbal auditory agnosia, so children may appear not to understand speech and can be mistaken for deaf
The EEG shows marked activation of epileptiform discharges during sleep, often reaching electrical status epilepticus in slow-wave sleep
Clinical seizures may be infrequent or absent, so the language regression and EEG findings are central to diagnosis
Behavioural disturbance and features overlapping with autism spectrum disorder commonly accompany the language loss
It lies on a continuum with the broader condition of epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep
Treatment aims to suppress the sleep-activated discharges, using antiseizure medication and corticosteroid or immunomodulatory therapy in resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: Landau-Kleffner syndrome is an epileptic encephalopathy in which intense epileptiform activity, markedly activated during non-REM sleep, disrupts the function of language-related cortical networks, particularly perisylvian regions. Continuous or near-continuous spike-wave discharges through slow-wave sleep are thought to interfere with the sleep-dependent consolidation and maturation of language and other higher functions, producing acquired aphasia and cognitive-behavioural regression even when overt seizures are few. The underlying cause is often unknown, with genetic and immune contributions implicated in some cases.
additionalDifferentials: Autism spectrum disorder with language regression
Acquired hearing loss or auditory processing disorder
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep (broader spectrum)
Other causes of acquired childhood aphasia (structural or inflammatory)
Selective mutism and psychiatric causes of language loss
additionalInvestigations: Sleep EEG or prolonged/overnight EEG to demonstrate electrical status epilepticus in slow-wave sleep
Formal audiological assessment to exclude deafness
Brain MRI to exclude a structural or inflammatory cause
Genetic and, where indicated, metabolic or autoimmune investigations
redFlags: Progressive loss of language and comprehension in a previously typical child
Electrical status epilepticus in slow-wave sleep on EEG
Marked behavioural or autistic regression accompanying language loss
Failure of language to recover despite apparent seizure control
reference.prognosis: Seizures, when present, usually remit by adolescence, but language and cognitive outcomes are variable and a significant proportion of children have persistent language or learning difficulties. Earlier recognition and effective suppression of the sleep-activated discharges are associated with better language recovery.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the child as deaf or as having primary autism and missing the EEG diagnosis
Relying on a routine awake EEG, which may miss the sleep-activated discharges
Judging treatment success by seizure control alone rather than language recovery
Delaying immunomodulatory or steroid therapy in resistant cases with ongoing regression
management: Suppress the sleep-activated epileptiform discharges with antiseizure medications such as valproate, levetiracetam, ethosuximide or benzodiazepines like clobazam
Use a course of corticosteroids or ACTH, or intravenous immunoglobulin, early and for a sustained period to try to reverse the language regression
Avoid antiseizure drugs that can aggravate the condition, such as carbamazepine and phenytoin
Provide intensive speech and language therapy with educational support and alternative or augmentative communication
Address the accompanying behavioural and autism-spectrum-like difficulties
Monitor with follow-up sleep EEG and serial language and neuropsychological assessment, coordinated through neurology, audiology and speech therapy
Consider epilepsy surgery such as multiple subpial transection in carefully selected refractory cases
